hplc.definition: A lab test that pushes a dissolved sample through a narrow column, so that different molecules come out at different times. It shows how pure a sample looks, but not by itself what the main substance is.

impurity.definition: Anything in a product that should not be there, such as faulty copies of the peptide, leftover chemicals from making it, or metals.

deletion-sequence.definition: A faulty copy of a peptide that misses one or more of its building blocks, or stops too early (a truncated sequence). It forms when a step in making the peptide does not finish.

iso-iec-17025.definition: An international standard for testing laboratories. A lab that is accredited to it has been checked by an outside body on how it works and tests.

batch-number.definition: A code on a medicine that shows which production run it came from. It lets a maker or regulator trace and recall a faulty batch.

syringe-units.definition: The marks on an insulin syringe. They measure an amount of liquid, made to fit insulin. They do not show how much of any other substance is in that liquid.

baseline.definition: A first measurement taken at the start, before anything changes. Later results are compared with it.

igf-1.definition: A growth factor in the blood that carries out many effects of growth hormone. Because it is steadier than growth hormone itself, doctors measure it to see how active growth hormone is.

full-blood-count.definition: A common blood test that counts red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. It can help find an infection, anaemia or a blood disorder.

anaemia.definition: Having too few red blood cells, or too little of the substance in them that carries oxygen. It can make you tired and short of breath.

liver-function-tests.definition: Blood tests that measure enzymes and other substances made or handled by the liver. An abnormal result can mean the liver is under stress, but more tests are needed to find the cause.

seh.definition: The hospital emergency department in the Netherlands. Unless a life is in danger, you go there only after the GP or huisartsenpost sends you.

nvic.definition: The Dutch poison information centre. It advises doctors, pharmacists and other professionals. If you think you are poisoned, call your GP or the huisartsenpost, and they can contact it.

landelijk-meldpunt-zorg.definition: The Dutch national reporting point of the health inspectorate (IGJ). You can report a doubtful website or seller of medicines there.

eigen-risico.definition: The part of your health care costs that you pay yourself each year in the Netherlands before your basic insurance pays. GP care does not count towards it; blood tests at a lab and hospital care do.

catalyst.definition: A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up. Some catalysts used to make peptides contain metals, so leftover metal must be tested for.

solvent.definition: A liquid used to dissolve other substances while a medicine is made. Small amounts can stay behind in the product, so they are tested for.

enzyme.definition: A protein that speeds up a chemical reaction in the body. When cells are damaged, some enzymes leak into the blood, where a blood test can measure them.

platelets.definition: Tiny cells in the blood that help it clot and stop bleeding.

yellow-card.definition: The UK system for reporting side effects and problems with medicines. It is run by the UK medicines regulator, the MHRA, and anyone can use it.

medwatch.definition: The US system for reporting side effects and problems with medicines to the FDA. Patients and health workers can both use it.

bfarm.definition: The German federal institute for medicines and medical devices. It runs an online portal where patients and health workers can report side effects.
